chunks: "The feedback network is the most sensitive part of a buck, so I treat it like a victim.
The divider goes right at the FB pin, so the high-impedance tap, the junction of the two resistors and the pin, is only a few millimetres of trace.
Its bottom resistor goes to the quiet analog ground at the IC, not into the noisy power return.
I keep the whole thing away from the switch node and the inductor, on the opposite side of the IC if I can, because both couple into it.
A femtofarad-scale capacitance from the switch node is enough: with 0.
1 picofarads to the switch node and 5 picofarads at the pin, a 12 volts edge puts about a quarter of a volt on a pin that's regulating to 0. 8 volts.
For the same reason I never run the FB tap trace under or beside the inductor, and I cross anything else at right angles.
If a long run is needed, I make it the sense line from the output, which is low impedance and driven by the output capacitors, and keep the tap short.
I take that sense line from the load side of the output capacitors, ideally at the load, so the regulator corrects for drop, and route it as a quiet trace, ideally over the ground plane.
Compensation and feed-forward parts hug their pins the same way. If the layout is cramped, I lower the divider resistance a bit, trading quiescent current for noise immunity."
